section.title: Jay Jo: Robinhood Promotions, GameStop, and Leaving Big Tech for Crypto
section.deck: Jay Jo describes a non-linear path from a Robinhood engineering role to a crypto startup, with views on risk, promotions and fundraising.

blocks.text: In Jay Jo's view, careers rarely move in a straight line; growth tends to arrive in step changes. Jay says the choice of job should follow what a person is optimizing for, such as pay or learning, and that the people around you are the biggest factor you can control. The conversation follows Jay from college internships to a fast-scaling Robinhood engineering role, a stretch of disengagement, and a move into crypto infrastructure. Jay argues that people are far too scared of leaving a job, because a competent engineer usually finds work again, and that a failed startup still builds skills employers value. Editorial note: the GameStop and company accounts are one insider's first-hand view and were not checked against outside sources.
blocks.heading: Jay Jo's view: careers move in steps, and people overrate the risk of leaving

blocks.question: How did Jay first get into big tech, and how much of it was luck?
answer: In college Jay wanted a brand-name internship at Facebook or Google, partly because that was what everyone else wanted. Jay was not strong at LeetCode-style problems, so Jay joined a friend's Friday-night problem-solving session. One problem from that session, counting islands in a grid, turned out to be the exact question in the second on-site interview for the Facebook internship. Jay calls the link a lucky coincidence, and says the offer shaped everything after it.
blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Were Google and Facebook the only prestigious places to intern?
answer: Jay says what people value depends on their circle. At UCLA, Google and Facebook were the reference points, but later other companies, including Palantir and some pre-IPO startups, came to be seen as just as prestigious.

followups.question: How did the Facebook internship compare with the Pinterest one?
answer: Jay found the Facebook internship impersonal. The Pinterest internship, a Kleiner Perkins fellowship in San Francisco, felt more personal, partly because its intern class was smaller. Jay is still close to four or five people from it, and few from the Facebook class.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why choose Robinhood over going back to Pinterest or doing a master's degree?
answer: Jay was about to graduate and weighed three options: returning to Pinterest, which Jay was less keen on since friends were not going back; a master's that UCLA offers with automatic admission from its fifth year; and small companies full of people doing significant work. Jay visited the Robinhood booth at the Greylock Tech Fair in 2017, where it had the longest line, and found a strong team.

In hindsight Jay says the master's would not have mattered, and the Robinhood role offered more. The new-grad class was unusually strong, and about a third of it later raised money. Rapid scaling exposed Jay to many problems, which Jay says sped up career growth.

followups.question: What stage was Robinhood at when Jay joined?
answer: Jay signed the offer at Series C and joined at Series D. At the offer stage the company had about 100 people across two nearby buildings, one of them a house where engineers worked at standing desks.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why choose a smaller company when big tech is the common advice?
answer: Jay says a person has to pick what they are optimizing for. Pay upside is rarely found at big tech, Jay argues, because the largest gains usually come from very early-stage companies. Learning is different: a smaller company that is growing quickly offers far more of it, though the path is high-variance, since a company can stop growing and the learning can dry up.
Jay says career growth at Robinhood ended up looking like a normal company's, though the learning was much better than expected.

followups.question: Does big tech carry the same reorganization risk?
answer: Jay says it depends on luck in any role. The biggest factor Jay can control is the people to work with, because a startup's prospects can shift fast even when it looks promising. Surrounding yourself with very smart people is a good heuristic for choosing where to go.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Did growth at Robinhood match what Jay expected?
answer: Jay says Jay joined a bit too late for the fast growth earlier hires got, and by then the company was already moving toward a more conventional big-company path. Jay missed the first review because of a late start, and went through the process at nine months, after long hours that sometimes ran until 2 a.m.
Jay also describes a painful on-call rotation, centered on an overnight batch process that ran after market close and sometimes went until 4 or 5 a.m., close to a business problem.

followups.question: What did the overnight batch work involve?
answer: Jay says the batch included trade settlement, which required coordinating with outside counterparties so every system matched. The jobs ran one after another, so a failure meant finding its cause, often a bad deployment, paging the engineer who wrote it, waiting for a fix, and rerunning the process.
Jay says the codebase was not architected in the most stable way and carried a lot of tech debt. Jay received a five-out-of-five performance rating, but no promotion or pay change followed.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Did that leave Jay jaded about big tech?
answer: Jay says the time put in did not match the reward. Jay considered becoming more checked out and going through the motions, a pattern Jay saw in many colleagues. That made Jay jaded about the big-tech environment and convinced Jay there was something bigger to work toward.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why stay about three and a half years if the frustration began after nine months?
answer: Jay says a family death made leaving harder, and stock options would have cost about $400,000 to exercise. Jay's plan was to stay until the options no longer had to be exercised before leaving, or until the IPO. The IPO came in July 2021, which Jay describes as removing the handcuffs, and Jay then went much deeper into crypto.

followups.question: Did staying pay off financially?
answer: Jay says the pay was an order of magnitude higher than three and a half years at a Google or Facebook type of company would have produced, and that the decision looks fantastic in hindsight. At the time, though, Jay felt locked in, which reduced happiness.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Was timing a factor?
answer: Jay says the group was lucky. Jay graduated in 2018, ahead of the 2021 wave of tech IPOs. Many friends at pre-IPO companies have still not listed, so their options may be worth little. Jay doubts a 2020 graduate would have had the same liquidity.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Was Jay promoted while doing only the minimum?
answer: Jay says Jay was promoted in the second performance cycle and was technically up for another promotion before leaving. By then Jay was putting in the bare minimum to stay close to average and spending time elsewhere.

Jay says that at a company that grew about tenfold, being a competent engineer made Jay the only person who knew many systems. That turned Jay into a domain expert and an engineering lead for several systems.

followups.question: In a fast-growing company, does competence alone make someone load-bearing?
answer: Jay agrees that when both the team and the workload grow, competence is rewarded almost automatically. Jay also mentored three people, the first about a year and a half into the job, which Jay says is much less common at larger companies.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: What was the GameStop episode like from inside Robinhood?
answer: Jay describes a stock frenzy in which about a dozen stocks, including GameStop and AMC, surged during the pandemic. Short sellers had to buy back shares, which pushed prices higher in a short squeeze. Robinhood was where many people traded, and on January 28, 2021 it turned off buying on those meme stocks. Jay learned about it on waking, and many contacts, some of them invested too, reached out that day.

followups.question: How did the episode affect Jay and the people around Jay?
answer: Jay says many contacts were upset as GameStop's price fell, and Jay felt powerless as an insider. The episode showed Jay how archaic the financial system is. Trades then took two days to settle, so Robinhood needed billions of dollars of collateral for open positions. Jay says that realization was one of the things that inspired the later startup.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Was the trading halt a deliberate move on the price?
answer: Jay says no. Robinhood turned off buys to raise collateral, not to influence the price, and Jay thinks the company miscommunicated the reason, possibly on purpose, while it was fundraising billions at the same time. Jay says the leaders were fighting for the company's existence with regulators already wary, and handled it in an okay way, but could have communicated much better.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Why did Jay leave to start something of Jay's own?
answer: Jay says Silicon Valley respects founders more than celebrities, so starting a company felt normal. The Kleiner Perkins fellowship, taken at age 21, made it seem accessible because many fellows had founded companies or were considering it. In 2019 Jay and a co-founder began building an AWS cost-management startup on nights and weekends.

followups.question: Why did that first startup not work out?
answer: Jay says cost management is a dull market, since fast-growing companies do not need to cut costs and stalling ones make poor customers. The startup found little traction, and Jay is glad not to have spent years on it. In 2021 the pair turned to crypto, aiming to build something like Robinhood in a decentralized way. They first built an on-chain order-book exchange, then realized the infrastructure underneath was the better thing to build.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: What did Jay need to see before going all in on the new company?
answer: Jay says a small team willing to work part-time, a good working relationship with the co-founder, and early excitement about the product were enough. Jay's bar was low because the IPO had just happened and Jay was near the end of a four-year grant, so there was little downside. Jay now calls it a fantastic time to make the move.

followups.question: Would Jay still have left with a middling pay package?
answer: Jay says it would have been even easier to leave, since the six months of equity given up was still a high dollar value to Jay. Jay thinks people are much too scared of leaving jobs. A competent person usually finds work again, and Jay does not know anyone who was good at one job and could not find another.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: If a startup fails, can someone simply go back?
answer: Jay says the main cost is opportunity cost. Building a product teaches validation, design, engineering, marketing and business development, which makes a person more valuable to employers. Seed-stage startups often value a former founder more than a typical engineer, since that person can have more impact in the zero-to-one phase. Jay adds that founders who fail often look at smaller companies next, partly by choice, and has seen people leave big tech, fail at a startup, and return to big tech.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: How did fundraising go for the company?
answer: Jay says the company raised about $35 million in total, starting with a $5 million seed round, followed by strategic rounds. The seed raise began about three weeks after the collapse of Terra, which Jay calls one of the worst times in crypto to raise money. Most investors said no, and Jay learned the full cycle: intro calls, partner meetings, and talks about the team, product and vision.

Jay says it was less frightening than expected. Investors start out skeptical, and once one fund is excited, others become easier to convince. Many stay on the sidelines to keep options open, giving reasons such as still doing diligence.

followups.question: How did Jay land a lead investor?
answer: Jay says a tier-one lead makes everything else easier. The team was introduced to top crypto investors, and Multicoin, which Jay says was the biggest early Solana investor, invested after good conversations. That credibility opened doors for business development, later fundraising and the launch.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: How is crypto fundraising different from traditional venture?
answer: Jay says crypto projects typically raise a seed round and a Series A, then hold a token launch, and seldom raise institutional rounds afterward. Web2 companies are judged on revenue and ARR, while crypto projects are judged on softer measures such as excitement and the number of teams building. Jay compares this to internet investing in about 1995 to 1997, when metrics like eyeball counts stood in for revenue.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Is crypto mostly grift, and what is the clear case for its value?
answer: Jay argues that any early industry attracts grift, and that the early internet had plenty of its own, with adult content arguably one of its biggest early uses. Jay expects grift to fade as regulation gives clearer rules and as social pressure makes investors wary of bad actors. Jay says AI is showing similar hype, with some companies raising money without building anything meaningful.

followups.question: Where does crypto deliver real value, in Jay's view?
answer: Jay says crypto has been strongest at payments and trading. A distributed ledger is expensive, because many machines repeat the same work, but it offers verifiability, which matters when real money is at stake. Jay points to stablecoins for international remittances, and to people in countries with rapidly inflating currencies who hold USDC or USDT, especially in Southeast Asia and Latin America. Jay expects verifiable computation between parties who do not trust each other to matter for many financial uses.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: Which period of Jay's career brought the most growth?
answer: Jay says 2022, the year Jay started the company, brought the most growth. Building alone means working through every problem without the support a job provides, and Jay says every year since has taught more than any earlier job.

followups.question: Are the most important lessons non-engineering ones?
answer: Jay says so. Engineering is generally the easier part of building a company, since most businesses solve fairly mundane problems rather than the scaling challenges of a company like Meta. Jay says a competent L4 engineer can do well as a founder in most engineering settings. Jay's main lessons were about starting a business and raising money.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

followups.question: Should a new graduate stay until technically competent before starting something?
answer: Jay says that if you know what you want to build, you should just go for it. Technical competence can be built or, more likely, hired for, and a good idea makes fundraising easier, which in turn makes it straightforward to grow a team.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: How has the company's team grown since it started?
answer: Jay says the company started in 2022 with five to seven people and now has around 60 full-time staff across its entities. Jay calls that lean growth relative to places like Robinhood and says it was the right decision, because slow growth keeps the culture intact and avoids bureaucracy and confusion about what to do.
blocks.speaker: Jay Jo

blocks.question: What would Jay tell a UCLA graduate, knowing what Jay knows now?
answer: Jay would say not to be so scared. Jay describes being naturally risk-averse and hesitant to take big leaps, unlike some people Jay knows. The best approach, Jay says, is to think through a decision and then pull the trigger quickly. Looking back, Jay should not have been so scared of leaving Robinhood, potentially even earlier.

followups.question: So in a perfect world, would Jay have left Robinhood sooner?
answer: Jay says yes in a perfect world, but is not sure things would have played out the same. Leaving earlier might have meant not starting the crypto company, and a cost-management startup would not have led to the same outcome.
followups.speaker: Jay Jo
